mainEntity.name: Does having chronic migraine mean I cannot have dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Chronic migraine is a neurological condition and does not, in isolation, prevent someone from being considered for dental implant treatment. What matters most is a thorough assessment of your overall health, the medications you are taking, your bone density, and your gum condition. Each patient's situation is different, and your dental team will evaluate all relevant factors before making any recommendations. It is always advisable to disclose your full medical history, including your migraine diagnosis and any treatments you are currently receiving.

mainEntity.name: Can migraine medication affect the success of dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some medications used to manage or prevent chronic migraine may have implications for implant treatment. For example, certain drugs can cause dry mouth, affect bone metabolism, or influence tissue healing. Topiramate, tricyclic antidepressants, and any medications affecting calcium or bone density are worth discussing specifically with your dentist. This does not mean implants are not possible, but your clinical team will want to understand the full picture to plan your treatment safely and appropriately.

mainEntity.name: Could dental treatment trigger a migraine episode?

acceptedAnswer.text: For some individuals, dental procedures — particularly those involving oral surgery, stress, or prolonged jaw opening — may act as a short-term trigger. This does not mean treatment should be avoided, but it is helpful to inform your dental team about your migraine pattern and any known triggers. With awareness and careful planning, treatment can often be timed and structured to minimise disruption. Your dental team may also suggest strategies for managing stress or discomfort around appointments.

mainEntity.name: Is dry mouth linked to migraine medication, and how does it affect my teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, several migraine medications — including tricyclic antidepressants and some anticonvulsants — can reduce saliva flow, a condition known as xerostomia or dry mouth. Saliva plays an important role in neutralising acids, washing away bacteria, and protecting tooth enamel. Reduced saliva significantly raises the risk of tooth decay and gum disease. These conditions, if present, need to be stabilised before implant treatment can begin. Your dentist can recommend appropriate products and strategies to manage dry mouth effectively.

mainEntity.name: What should I tell my dentist if I have chronic migraine?

acceptedAnswer.text: You should inform your dentist of your migraine diagnosis, how frequently you experience episodes, all medications you take (including any over-the-counter pain relief), and any other health conditions you manage. It is also helpful to mention whether you experience jaw pain, teeth grinding, or facial discomfort, as these may be relevant to your dental assessment. The more your dentist understands about your health, the better placed they are to provide safe, personalised, and effective care.

mainEntity.name: Are there alternatives to implants if I am not suitable?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. If a clinical assessment determines that dental implants are not currently suitable — for any reason — there are other tooth replacement options that your dentist may discuss with you. These include fixed bridgework, which uses adjacent teeth as anchors, and removable dentures. Each option has its own advantages and limitations, and the most appropriate choice depends on your individual oral health, bone structure, and personal preferences. Your dentist will guide you through the options available based on your specific circumstances.
